description.narrative:
Somalia’s urban IDP settlements reveals a systemic failure of conventional humanitarian models to adapt to highly mobile populations. In Banadir region, which hosts over 600,000 IDPs (IOM DTM, May 2024), static clinics (health facilities) and protection facilities cannot effectively serve rapid shifting informal settlements. Critical gaps persist seen in fragmented access whereby 65% of IDP households in Mogadishu must travel to three or more locations to access essential health, nutrition, and protection services (REACH,2023). This imposes prohibitive time, cost, and safety burdens especially on women and female-headed households.
Despite Ministry of Health efforts, vaccination dropout rates exceed 40% in peri-urban IDP sites (WHO Health Cluster, Q12024). Population mobility and distance to clinics are primary drivers of low coverage. Concurrently, women and girls face elevated risks of gender-based violence, yet static Women and Girls’ Friendly Spaces (WGFS) remain underutilized in new or remote settlements due to insecure routes and social stigma (2024 HNO). The core challenge is a structural mismatch between static service provision and dynamic displacement realities. This pilot addresses this systems failure by introducing a nimble, integrated,mobile service hub designed to deliver health, protection, and nutrition interventions directly to fluid IDP communities, ensuring continuity of care, reducing access barriers, andenhancing safety for vulnerable groups.
The “Nabad Mobile Hub” pilotsahyper-efficient, data-informed mobile service delivery unit.Its innovation lies in its predictive targeting mechanism and deep vertical integration of services at a single touchpoint, directly countering identified systemic gaps. Technical Uniqueness 1.Predictive Targeting via Multi-Source Data Fusion Methodology: Deployment is optimized using a composite vulnerability index that weighs and integrates three real-time data streams: 1. MoH Health SystemData: Sub-district level data on Pentavalent-3 vaccination coverage (<(><<)>50%) and global acute malnutrition (GAM) prevalence (>15%) from the DHIS2 platform. 2. IOM-DTM Emergency Trend Tracking: Alerts on new arrival locations and estimated numbers within the last 14-day reporting cycle. 3. Community-Defined Vulnerability: CDMCs use a simple SMS-based alert system to flag new informal settlements and specific protection concerns. This is integrated in the current DAWA’s CFRM SMS hotline system. 2. Vertical Integration of Services Protocol: The hub operates on an integrated service protocol, co-designed with MoH and Protection Cluster technical leads, to provide:  Health: Routine immunization (leveraging MoH's cold chain), MUAC screening.  Protection: A dedicated, private WGFS module staffed by female trained volunteers providing psychosocial first aid (PFA), safe identification and referral of GBV cases (using the Inter-Agency GBV Case Management Guidelines).  Linkages with other FSL intervention: A "While You Wait" digital registration point for caregivers, pre-registering them for longer-term VSLAs or multipurpose cash programs, addressing a key socioeconomic driver of vulnerability.
Assumptions • Predictive targeting based on multi-source data fusion enables faster deployment to new IDPsites. • Co-located health, protection, and nutrition services reduce access barriers, especially for women. • Combining services increases trust and cross-sectoral engagement (e.g., GBV identification during health visits).
The project will henceforthbeimplemented over a 12-month period through four sequential phases, each led by DAWA in coordination with MoH, IOM, and community stakeholders. The intervention aims to directly benefit 2,160 children aged 3–12 and 1,200 women and adolescent girls across two high-density displacement sites in the Banadir region. These sites are selected based on population flow data and service access gaps .
The targetingstrategy is designed to ensure inclusive, equitable representation of vulnerable subgroups, in alignment with humanitarian protection standards and accountability to affected populations (AAP) principles.

participating-org.narrative: DAWA Somalia is an Local humanitarian and development organization committed to promoting the welfare and well-being of vulnerable communities across Somalia. DAWA plays a crucial role in the organization’s broader vision of promoting humanitarian aid, sustainable development, and social justice in regions affected by poverty, conflict, and underdevelopment. Established as part of DAWA’s commitment to serving the Somali people. DAWA’s Vision is Restoring dignity and harmony to the lives of those affected by humanitarian crises, displacement, and poverty while their Mission is addressing poverty and its root causes by developing comprehensive solutionsthat empower individuals and their communities. DAWA responds to emergencies by providing critical support such as food, clean water, medical supplies, and shelter to those affected by drought, famine, conflict, and other crises. DAWA’s rapid response efforts have been instrumental in saving lives and reducing suffering Understanding the importance of education in breaking the cycle of poverty, DAWA has prioritized the construction and rehabilitation of schools, the provision of educational materials, and the training of teachers. These efforts aim to increase access to quality education for children and youth in Somalia DAWA operates and supports several healthcare facilities across Somalia, offering essential medical services, maternal and child health programs, vaccination campaigns, and health education. These initiatives are vital in improving health outcomes and reducing mortality rates in the region. Topromote self-reliance and reduce poverty, DAWA implements various livelihood projects, including vocational training, small business support, and agricultural development programs. These initiatives are designed to empower individuals, particularly women and youth, to achieve economic independence. In Somalia, the urgent need for clean water affects millions, worsening health issues and hindering development. The community’s daily struggle withwater shortages underscores a serious crisis and DAWA is committed to providingsustainable water solutions to alleviate suffering, improve well- being, and build resilience. The success of DAWA is bolstered by strong partnerships with local communities,government agencies, international organizations, and UN agencies. These collaborations ensure that DAWA’s programs are culturally sensitive, locally relevant, and effectively address the needs of the Somali people.
